tagline.text: A northern Negros volcano with a hidden-sea caldera and sulfur fields

location.label: Location
location.text: Northern Negros Occidental, inside Northern Negros Natural Park (around Silay, Talisay and Murcia)

children.text: Mount Mandalagan is a complex volcano rising about 1,885 m inside Northern Negros Natural Park. With Tinagong Dagat, a caldera plain whose name means "hidden sea," a sulfur fumarole field and rainforest trekking, it is one of Negros's signature hikes.
Mount Mandalagan sits in northwestern Negros, inside Northern Negros Natural Park about
40km
northeast of Bacolod. According to Wikipedia it is a complex stratovolcano about
high, with seven volcanic centers, at least five craters or calderas, and a base about
26km

across. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) classes it as potentially active, and the date of its last eruption is unknown. Locals also call it Nahigda nga Babayi, meaning "the lying woman."
The heart of the route most hikers actually walk is Tinagong Dagat, a caldera plain at about

. The name means "hidden sea." In the wet season the broad plain floods and looks like a lake, while in the dry season the water drains away and it turns into grassland and a campsite. Mist drifting across the basin, which is about
2km
wide, makes for the mountain's finest morning view. Walking east from here brings you to Solfatara, a zone of boiling sulfur and bubbling mud, and in the other direction lies Marapara Peak (about
), the highest point reachable on the trail.

Northern Negros Natural Park began as a forest reserve in 1935 and became a natural park in 2005, covering about 80,000 hectares. It shelters Visayan endemic species such as deer and warty pigs, along with rare birds like the Visayan hornbill, and old-growth forest survives above

. Entry is therefore not free. You must follow the park office (NNNP) rules on climbing permits, mandatory guides and porters, and weekly visitor limits, and the protected area operates on a zero-waste principle.

Many people say it is easier than Mount Kanlaon, also on Negros, but with a long distance and leech-ridden rainforest sections it is not a casual stroll. The usual approach is to fly from Manila or Cebu to Bacolod-Silay Airport and meet your guide in Silay City, so it fits into a long weekend. It makes a distinctive nature add-on to a Bacolod city visit or a trip to the La Carlota area.
This crater plain at about
is named the "hidden sea." Water rises in the wet season and the grass reappears in the dry season, like a tide, so the scenery looks completely different from one season to the next.

In the dry season the plain dries out and is wide enough for hundreds of tents. After dark there is almost no light, so the stars pour out, and at dawn mist flows through the basin, which makes it good for photos.
About
2 hours

on foot east of Tinagong Dagat, there is an area of sulfur fumaroles and boiling mud. You can feel that this is a potentially active volcano, but gas and hot ground mean you must follow your guide's instructions.
The highest point reachable on the trail, at about
. The final stretch is steep and thickly overgrown, so go with an experienced guide, and bring plenty of drinking water because there is none near the top.
Mossy rainforest begins right at the start, with highland trees such as almaciga along the way. Long stretches with birdsong and streams make it a good fit for travelers who enjoy observing nature.

You can climb from Campuestuhan in Talisay, Patag in Silay or Canlandog in Murcia, and the park office rotates the assigned trail week by week. You can also do a traverse, going up one trail and down another.

Northern Negros Natural Park is recorded as home to rare animals such as the Visayan spotted deer, Visayan warty pig, Negros shrew, Visayan hornbill and Negros bleeding-heart. They are not easy to see, but there is pleasure in walking while your guide explains the forest.

items.title: 1 night, 2 days traverse
items.subtitle: Up from Campuestuhan, camp at Tinagong Dagat, down to Patag

children.text: Travel from Bacolod-Silay Airport or Bacolod city to Silay City, stay overnight, and confirm details with the park office and your guide. Get your permit in advance.
Start from the Campuestuhan trailhead in Barangay Cabatangan, Talisay. A park office staff member checks the headcount and your list of trash items.
You pass the ranger station at about
. The forest path is fairly gentle up to here.
You reach a rest area at about
, where you can refill water and have a snack.
You pass a small dam at about
. There are several springs along the way, but do not use soap or detergent near water sources.
Have lunch at the rest area at about
and prepare for the final climb.
Descend into the Tinagong Dagat basin and pitch your tent at the campsite at about
. In the wet season, camp along the edge of the basin away from the flooded plain.
Have dinner, look at the stars, and turn in early. Lights-out is usually early here.
After breakfast, pack up the tent and begin the descent toward Patag.
You pass the Marapara Peak junction at about
. If you want to go to the summit and back, agree on the extra time with your guide.
Pass the Diwal point at about
and continue down through the forest.
Reach the Patag trailhead at about
and take a jeepney to Silay.
These times are an example based on a group trek record written in August 2023. The trailhead is assigned weekly by the park office, so confirm it first, and times vary with weather and group size.

items.title: Day trip to Tinagong Dagat
items.subtitle: Round trip from the Patag trailhead

children.text: Travel from Bacolod to Silay by bus or van.
In Silay, charter a jeepney or take a regular jeepney to the Patag trailhead.
Start trekking and pass the Alimatok camp area.
Arrive at Tinagong Dagat, have lunch and enjoy the view of the basin.
Start the descent by the same route.
Reach the trailhead and return by jeepney via Silay to Bacolod.

This course is an example from a 2012 trek record, and under today's protected-area rules the permit and mandatory-guide conditions may differ. Recent guides and trip reports treat an overnight camp as the norm, so check with the park office first whether a same-day round trip is allowed.

items.title: 2 nights, 3 days Marapara and Solfatara
items.subtitle: Tinagong Dagat, sulfur field, Marapara Peak

children.text: Enter the park, have lunch at Tinagong Dagat, then walk east to the Solfatara sulfur field and camp.
Return to Tinagong Dagat and head toward Marapara Peak, camping on a small flat spot near the top. There is no water on this section, so carry plenty of drinking water.
Traverse toward Talisay and descend. Information on this section is scarce, so discuss it with your guide beforehand.
This is an extended course for experienced hikers. Check beforehand that the park office allows it and that your guide knows the way.
Several direct flights a day connect Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) with Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
From the airport it takes about
20–30 minutes
by taxi or van to central Bacolod, and less to central Silay.
On an early flight you can reach Silay the same day, find a place to stay and start the hike early the next morning.
Flights and fares change with the season, so check the latest timetable before booking.
There are ferry and bus combinations from Manila via Iloilo or Cebu to Bacolod, but they take a long time and are not recommended for travelers with a short schedule.
From Cebu, you can take a ferry such as OceanJet or 2GO to a port serving Bacolod. Check timetables locally.
Buses and vans to Silay run frequently from Bacolod's northern terminal and take about
30 minutes to 1 hour
One group trek record lists the van from Bacolod to Silay at about
. Fares change, so confirm when you board.
From Bacolod airport to Silay you can use Grab or a taxi.
The Patag trailhead is an unpaved uphill road, so an SUV or pickup truck is suitable. Ordinary passenger cars are not recommended.
An older record says regular jeepneys from Silay run irregularly between about 9 a.m. and 3–4 p.m., and a chartered jeepney is convenient for groups.
The Campuestuhan trailhead is on the Talisay side and close to Bacolod, but first check with the park office which trailhead is currently assigned.
The jeepney fares recorded in 2012 were about
(regular) and
(charter). This is old information, so confirm current fares locally.

The dry season from November to May is the best time to walk Mount Mandalagan. The trails are less slippery, there are fewer leeches, and the Tinagong Dagat plain is dry, leaving plenty of room for tents.

June to October is the wet season, with frequent rain, and the plain floods like a lake, giving the scenery that best matches the name "hidden sea." On the other hand, the trails are muddy, leeches and lightning become more of a risk, and camping is limited to the edges. Either way, the park office sets your entry date, so plan ahead.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Peak season with clear skies, good for stars and sunrise. Mornings are chilly, so bring warm clothing.
The plain is dry and camping is easy, but it is hot outside the forest at midday. Bring plenty of water.
Wet season, frequent rain and mist
The plain floods and trails are slippery. Leeches are plentiful, and a typhoon can close the trail.

Staying in central Silay before and after the hike is the most convenient option. Silay is a heritage city with surviving Spanish-era houses, so it is a good place to tour old homes and eat after the descent. An older record mentions rooms and dormitory beds in a rest-house building called the "Hospital" at the Patag trailhead, but current operation and rates must be confirmed locally.

There are no restaurants on the mountain, so bring your own food such as packed meals, instant rice, noodles and energy bars. Guides sometimes build a fire and cook for you, so for a group trek agree on the menu beforehand. After the descent, many people head back to Bacolod for Negrense food such as chicken inasal or piaya.

Start preparing your climbing permit several weeks ahead. Send the booking form to the park office; you may need an individual information form, a notarized waiver, a medical certificate, an online orientation certificate and a zero-waste commitment form. Requirements can change, so check the latest notice.
Records say groups are limited to 15 people and 30 climbers per week, so dates fill up fast in peak season. Fix your date first, then book your flight.
There are several springs, but water at Tinagong Dagat depends on the weather. Bring a water filter or purification tablets, and carry plenty of water for Marapara Peak, where there is none.
To guard against leeches, wear long socks and trousers, and bring leggings that cover the ankles or insect repellent. Take care that none get onto your eyes or face.
A record says phone signal is available only in some sections such as the Alimatok rest area, and there is no data at the campsite. Tell your family your plan and download offline maps.
Trash such as plastic is counted on entry and checked on exit, so cut down on outer packaging before you bring it.
Bring warm clothing, a waterproof jacket and a waterproof cover for your sleeping bag. Nights in the basin are cold and damp from mist and dew.
A record says the Silay tourism office is closed on weekends and holidays, so it is best to make inquiries on weekdays.
Mount Mandalagan is a potentially active volcano and a protected area. Do not enter without a permit, and at the Solfatara sulfur field do not go beyond the places your guide allows.
Leeches live along the whole forest trail. Once one attaches, twist it off by hand rather than using salt or fire, and disinfect the spot.
A record says there are many beehives on the mountain and the bees can turn aggressive when locals harvest honey. If you see a hive, quietly avoid it following your guide's instructions.
The route to Marapara Peak is steep and overgrown, and a record says guides know the Tinagong Dagat side better. Explain your route to them in detail beforehand.
In the wet season the trails are slippery, and lightning or gusts are dangerous, so check the weather forecast and postpone if necessary.
Because of sulfur gas and hot ground, people with weak lungs and children should not go close to Solfatara.
A heritage city with surviving Spanish-era houses and a cathedral, close to the Patag trailhead and a good place to stay before and after the hike. It is about
30 minutes to 1 hour
by car from Bacolod.
The central city of Negros Occidental, with food such as chicken inasal and convenient airport connections. A good place to rest after the hike.
The ruins of a mansion built by a sugar baron, famous for its view around dusk. If you descend on the Talisay side it is close by, so the two combine well.
A hot-spring and waterfall resort on the northwest slope of Mount Kanlaon, showing a different face of Negros's mountains.
